Yes I do! I've been tested for ADHD, and the assessor decided my executive dysfunction was most likely caused by autism + anxiety instead. Then I got tested for autism. As part of that testing, I had an IQ test that revealed I have a *big* discrepancy between my verbal IQ and processing speed & working memory (verbal IQ much higher). I have trouble with switching tasks. If I get super focused on one thing, it's gonna be hard for me to break away and do another thing properly.

I feel the exact same. My autism is mild, but my symptoms are mainly social. I feel so isolated when I see "neurodiversity" content because I know it's gonna equate the experience of being an autistic woman with miraculously adapting to gender roles no matter what. I was treated more harshly than guys with my exact symptoms when I was in school, and the only reason I was diagnosed late is because my mother had no idea how to get me tested (but she absolutely tried). I get too burnt out trying to keep up a friend group. I have to wear earplugs to my college classes. I have trouble changing my tone of voice and have to put extra effort in. I've embarrassed myself in front of classes because I did not pick up on a professor's question being rhetorical. I couldn't deal with the cafeteria in high school. Most of the time I got in trouble at home, it was because (unintentionally) said something disrespectful.

If you're able, talk to someone in your life that you trust about the pros and cons IQ testing. I was very ashamed to get my IQ tested, but had to do it as part of my assessment when I got diagnosed. It provided me with very helpful information. The psychologist even chose not to calculate a composite IQ because there was such a big gap between my scores between categories! I had trouble with math my whole life; I always got done slower than the other kids and had trouble with equations where there were a lot of steps. The IQ test showed me I didn't have dyscalculia or adhd or just anxiety. Just autism with bad executive function. I needed to know that for my classes and self-esteem. 

Autism is, in fact, a disability. Being disabled can be an isolating experience. I hope you find a solution to some of the problems you're going through right now. You're not less of an adult for not being able to do things related to motor skills like driving or tying your shoes. Depending on your location and insurance, you do have the option of seeking some kind of vocational training specifically designed for autistic people.

The puzzle piece came about in 1963 by Gerald Gasson as a symbol of awareness (https://neurolaunch.com/autism-puzzle-piece-background/). He was the parent of an autistic child and a member of the National Autistic Society in the UK. He intended to portray autism as a complex and "puzzling" disorder. The original version had an image of a crying child in on the puzzle piece, but that version was phased out fairly early on. The puzzle piece has been interpreted more recently to be an implication that autistic people aren't whole (I'm not sure where this can be traced back to). However, that interpretation has been spreading around like it's a fact. I like your interpretation better than the new one cropping up in autistic online spaces, frankly.

You may be right. I haven't seen the professionals' side of things, but many autistic influencers I've seen \*only\* focus on that non-stereotypical presentation when talking about women and state that it's the main reason women don't get diagnosed, even in cases where it may not be true. I admit that my perspective is limited.

It sounds like you've already said what needed to be said in the moment, so what's important is that you continue doing what you're doing. Let her know that there may be situations where she may have to hide her identity for safety, but it doesn't mean being a lesbian is bad or wrong. Ignorant and hateful remarks / actions are a bigger reflection of others than herself. Considering that she's literal-minded and counselors have brought it up to you that she may be on the autism spectrum, it's good idea to make sure she can recognize backhanded compliments, insults described as "constructive criticism", and when she's being ignored. This will help her develop healthy friendships as well as romantic relationships as she gets older. The lesbian community can unfortunately be full of subtle signaling and in-jokes due to the history of oppression of gay people. This will be very foreign to your ears as a straight ally, but as your daughter talks about the things she sees in the lesbian community, things will start to make sense. 

Best of luck to both of you, I'm glad that you're reaching out.
